en: Extremely miserable or hopeless; completely without pride or dignity
hook: AB-JECT: thrown (ject) away (ab), cast down to the lowest point.
story: Abject. Extremely miserable or hopeless; completely without pride or dignity. After river erosion swallowed his family's land, Sam lived for a season in abject poverty, sleeping under plastic sheets on an embankment and eating one meal a day. Yet he never stopped going to school. Today he teaches in the same district, and he still remembers those abject months. Ab means away and ject means thrown, as in reject, so abject means thrown away, cast down to the lowest point. So, what word describes misery so deep it feels completely hopeless? ... Abject.

gre.s: Far from the defiant statement his supporters expected, the senator issued an ____ apology, begging forgiveness and conceding every one of his critics' points.
gre.clue: begging forgiveness and conceding every one of his critics' points

example: Caught copying his lab report, Rafi sent the professor an abject email that apologized four times in three short paragraphs.

en: Distant and unfriendly; emotionally reserved
hook: ALOOF: sits ALOFT on the ROOF, far above everyone.
story: Aloof. Distant and unfriendly; emotionally reserved. When a new boy named Zeke joined Frank's class, he sat alone, answered in single words, and never joined the cricket at lunch. Everyone thought he was proud and aloof. Then Frank learned that Zeke's father had just lost his job, and the boy was simply shy and sad. The next day, Frank asked him to bat first. Aloof began as a sailor's word for keeping a ship away from the shore, so an aloof person keeps away from others. So, what word describes someone who stays cool and distant? ... Aloof.

gre.s: Although the actress appeared ____ in interviews, rarely smiling or revealing anything personal, her friends describe her as warm and playful.
gre.clue: rarely smiling or revealing anything personal

example: The new striker stayed aloof from his teammates during training, eating lunch alone and skipping the squad's evening card games.

en: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something
hook: AMBI = both (ambidextrous). Feeling BOTH ways at once.
story: Ambivalent. Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something. When Mason got a job offer in Singapore, his mother was ambivalent. She was proud that her son had done so well, and she told every neighbour about it. But at night she [sigh] thought of his empty room and wondered who would eat her mango pickle now. Ambi means both, as in ambidextrous, and valent means strength, so ambivalent means feeling two strong pulls at once. So, what word describes feeling both happy and sad about the same thing? ... Ambivalent.

gre.s: The critic remained ____ about the novel, admiring its lyrical prose while deploring its sluggish, aimless plot.
gre.clue: admiring its lyrical prose while deploring

example: Nusrat felt ambivalent about the job offer in Chittagong, eager for the higher salary but reluctant to leave her parents in Dhaka.

en: Friendly and without serious disagreement
hook: AMICABLE: AMIGO (friend) + able.
story: Amicable. Friendly and without serious disagreement. Two brothers in a quiet town had to divide the family land and house. The neighbours expected shouting and lawyers, as so often happens. Instead, the brothers sat on the veranda over tea, walked the fields together, and agreed on every boundary in a single afternoon. Their mother cried with relief. It was a completely amicable settlement. Amicable comes from amicus, the Latin for friend, like amigo in Spanish. So, what word describes an agreement reached in a friendly way? ... Amicable.

gre.s: Although the negotiations had been tense, the two companies reached an ____ settlement, parting on such good terms that they later launched a joint venture.
gre.clue: parting on such good terms that they later launched a joint venture

example: The two neighbors ended their long quarrel over the shared wall with an amicable chat over tea on the rooftop.

en: Obscure and puzzling, familiar only to a small group of specialists
hook: ARCANE: hidden in an ARK, like secret knowledge only priests can read.
story: Arcane. Obscure and puzzling, familiar only to a small group of specialists. In a back room of the county land office, Rob's uncle spends his days reading old land records full of Persian terms. Old record terms mean nothing to most people, but he reads a century-old deed as easily as a newspaper. To everyone else, it is arcane knowledge. Arcane comes from the Latin for a chest or box, the same root as ark, so arcane knowledge is locked away for the few. So, what word describes knowledge so obscure that only specialists understand it? ... Arcane.

gre.s: The scholar's knowledge of ____ medieval manuscripts, which perhaps a dozen people in the world could read, made her indispensable to the museum.
gre.clue: which perhaps a dozen people in the world could read

example: The tax code is so arcane that even experienced accountants in Motijheel sometimes phone colleagues to interpret a single clause.

en: Very strict or serious; extremely plain, without comfort or decoration
hook: AUSTERE sounds like 'a stair' of bare concrete: no carpet, no decoration, just hard steps.
story: Austere. Very strict or serious; also, extremely plain, without comfort or decoration. Alan's grandfather lived in an austere room: a wooden bed, one chair, a shelf of books and a single bulb. No television, no carpet. He rose at dawn, ate plain rice and dal, and wasted nothing. Alan used to find it sad. Now, as a stressed young banker, he [sigh] sometimes envies that austere peace. Think of austerity, when a government cuts every luxury: austere means stripped down to bare needs. So, what word describes a life or room that is very plain and strict? ... Austere.

gre.s: In contrast to the lavish palaces of his predecessors, the new ruler's residence was strikingly ____, furnished with little more than a desk and a cot.
gre.clue: In contrast to the lavish palaces

example: The physics department occupied an austere concrete building with bare walls, metal chairs, and a single flickering lamp in each corridor.

en: Able to stay afloat; lighthearted and hopeful about the future
hook: BUOYANT: like a BUOY, always floating up.
story: Buoyant. Able to stay afloat; also, lighthearted and hopeful. At his first swimming lesson in the village pond, Nell's little brother clung to a raft of banana trunks, terrified. The trunks were so buoyant that they floated even with him on top, and soon he was kicking and [laugh] laughing. He came home in a buoyant mood, telling everyone he would swim across the great river one day. A buoy floats up on the water, and a buoyant person's spirits float up the same way. So, what word describes something that floats, or a mood that stays light and hopeful? ... Buoyant.

gre.s: Investors remained ____ despite the gloomy forecasts, convinced that the economy would rebound within a few months and reward those who held their nerve.
gre.clue: convinced that the economy would rebound within a few months

example: Despite losing the first two matches, the team's mood stayed buoyant, and the players joked loudly on the bus back to Sylhet.

en: Able to burn or corrode chemically; sarcastically bitter and hurtful
hook: CAUSTIC soda burns your skin; caustic words burn your feelings.
story: Caustic. Able to burn chemically; also, sarcastically bitter and hurtful. In the chemistry lab, the teacher warned Isabelle never to touch caustic soda, because it burns the skin. That evening, at a family gathering, an aunt glanced at Isabelle's results and said, "Only seventy marks? Your cousin got ninety, and she hardly studies." The caustic remark stung far longer than any chemical. Caustic comes from the Greek for burning, so caustic words burn feelings the way caustic soda burns skin. So, what word describes a comment that is bitter and hurtful? ... Caustic.

gre.s: The reviewer's ____ wit, which spared neither the actors nor the director, made her columns as feared as they were entertaining.
gre.clue: spared neither the actors nor the director

example: The chemistry teacher warned the class that the caustic solution could burn skin within seconds and insisted everyone wear gloves.

en: A puzzling problem that has no easy answer
hook: CONUNDRUM: a DRUM of confusion banging in your head.
story: Conundrum. A puzzling problem that has no easy answer. Travis won two scholarships in the same week: one to study engineering in Germany, the other to study medicine at home, close to his parents. Both were dreams. That night he sat on the roof, [sigh] watching the city lights and turning it over in his head. It was a real conundrum, with no easy answer. Picture a drum of confusion banging inside your head: that is a conundrum. So, what word names a puzzling problem with no easy answer? ... Conundrum.

gre.s: The dwindling water supply poses a genuine ____ for officials: restricting use would anger farmers, yet doing nothing would leave the city dry within a decade.
gre.clue: restricting use would anger farmers, yet doing nothing would leave the city dry

example: Choosing a university became a real conundrum for Tanvir, since the best program was abroad but his family could not afford the fees.

en: To reduce or cut short
hook: CUR-TAIL: cut the TAIL short.
story: Curtail. To reduce or cut short. When fuel prices rose sharply, Carl's family had to curtail their spending. No more Friday dinners at the Chinese restaurant, fewer new clothes for the holidays, and the air conditioner switched off before midnight. Carl's mother even curtailed her long phone calls to her sister. They managed, and they grew closer around the dinner table. Hear the word tail inside curtail, and picture a long tail being cut short. So, what verb means to cut something back or cut it short? ... Curtail.

gre.s: Fearing a budget shortfall, the university was forced to ____ its research programs, eliminating nearly a third of them.
gre.clue: eliminating nearly a third of them

example: Repeated power cuts curtailed evening study hours at the dormitory, so students began gathering under the streetlights to finish their homework.

en: To reduce the value or quality of something
hook: DE-TRACT: TRACT (pull) value AWAY.
story: Detract. To reduce the value or quality of something. Jessie's wedding photographs were beautiful: a red sari, marigolds, soft evening light. But in the background of every picture hung a tangle of electric wires and a rusty water tank. Her photographer [chuckle] promised to edit them out, because they detracted from the beauty of the day. Tract comes from the Latin for pull, as in tractor, and de means away, so to detract is to pull value away. So, what verb means to take away from something's value or beauty? ... Detract.

gre.s: A few minor typographical errors do little to ____ from what is otherwise a meticulously researched and elegantly written history.
gre.clue: otherwise a meticulously researched and elegantly written history

example: The noisy air conditioner detracted from an otherwise moving concert, drowning out the softest passages of the sitar solo.

en: Deep hostility; the state of being enemies
hook: ENMITY: ENEMY-ity.
story: Enmity. Deep hostility; the state of being enemies. For thirty years, two families in a farming village had not spoken. A quarrel over a mango tree on the boundary had grown into an enmity that their grandchildren inherited without knowing why. Then the floods came, and one family's boat was the only one left. They rescued their neighbours without a word, and the old enmity simply melted on the water. Enmity is built from enemy: the state of being enemies. So, what word names a long, deep hostility between people? ... Enmity.

gre.s: The ____ between the two clans, rooted in a dispute over land generations earlier, was so bitter that members refused even to attend the same weddings.
gre.clue: so bitter that members refused even to attend the same weddings

example: Years of open enmity ended only when the two retired tennis champions, once bitter rivals, agreed to coach the national youth squad together.

en: Short-lived; fading or disappearing soon after it appears
hook: EPHEMERAL: like an Instagram story, gone in a day.
story: Ephemeral. Short-lived; fading soon after it appears. On winter mornings, fog covers the hillside tea gardens, and drops of dew shine on the leaves like tiny diamonds. Piper [gasp] stopped on the path to photograph them. By nine o'clock the sun had burned the mist away, and the diamonds were gone. Such beauty is ephemeral. Ephemeral comes from the Greek for lasting only a day, so ephemeral things are here today and gone tomorrow. So, what word describes beauty that fades almost as soon as it appears? ... Ephemeral.

gre.s: Unlike the ____ fashions that vanish within a season, the designer's classic coat has remained popular for over fifty years.
gre.clue: vanish within a season

example: Most viral dance trends are ephemeral, filling every phone screen in Dhaka for a week before they are forgotten entirely.

en: Unreasonably high, especially of price
hook: EX-ORBIT-ANT: prices gone OUT OF ORBIT.
story: Exorbitant. Unreasonably high, especially of price. Two days before the holiday, Stan tried to buy a bus ticket home. The man at the counter shrugged and asked for three times the normal fare. Stan [gasp] stared at him. Every ticket left in the city had an exorbitant price. In the end, he [sigh] shared a minibus with five other students. Ex means out of and orbita means track, so an exorbitant price has jumped right out of its normal track. So, what word describes a price that is unreasonably high? ... Exorbitant.

gre.s: Many families who once used the private clinic now avoid it, since its ____ fees put even routine checkups beyond the reach of ordinary workers.
gre.clue: put even routine checkups beyond the reach of ordinary workers

example: The landlord demanded an exorbitant deposit of six months' rent, so the young couple kept searching for another flat in Mirpur.

en: To flatter or please someone excessively to gain favor
hook: FAWN: like a puppy wagging its tail, licking boots.
story: Fawn. To flatter or please someone excessively to gain favour. When the company director visited the port city branch, one officer rushed to carry his bag, laughed loudly at every joke, and praised even his tie. The other staff exchanged quiet glances. They had seen him fawn over every boss who ever visited. Picture a puppy wagging its tail and licking your shoes for a biscuit: that is how a fawning person behaves. Do not confuse it with a fawn, the baby deer. So, what verb means to flatter someone too much to win their favour? ... Fawn.

gre.s: Whenever the visiting director appeared, the junior staff would ____, laughing politely at his weakest jokes and praising his every remark, while the senior engineers remained coolly professional.
gre.clue: praising his every remark

example: Reporters who fawned over the billionaire at his product launch later struggled to ask him any hard questions about his company's debts.

en: Done openly and shamelessly, so the wrong is impossible to miss
hook: FLAGRANT: as obvious as a FLAG waving in your face.
story: Flagrant. Done openly and shamelessly, so the wrong is impossible to miss. In a school cricket match, the bowler stepped far over the line, a clear no-ball, and the batsman was caught. Yet the umpire, who happened to be the bowler's uncle, raised his finger and gave the batsman out. The crowd went silent, then booed. It was a flagrant act of favouritism. Flagrant comes from the Latin for blazing, so a flagrant wrong blazes in plain sight. So, what word describes wrongdoing that is shameless and impossible to miss? ... Flagrant.

gre.s: Far from being a subtle oversight, the company's dumping of chemicals into the river was a ____ violation of environmental law, carried out openly in daylight for years.
gre.clue: carried out openly in daylight for years

example: The referee sent off the defender for a flagrant foul, a reckless late tackle that left the striker lying on the grass.

en: To do without something pleasant; to give up
hook: FOR-GO: let it GO.
story: Forgo. To do without something pleasant; to give up. Every holiday, Lena's family buys new clothes. This year, after floods destroyed the home of her school's cleaner, Lena decided to forgo her new dress and gave the money to his family instead. Her mother said nothing, only held her close. In forgo, for means away, so to forgo something is to let it go away. Do not mix it up with forego, which means to go before. So, what verb means to give up something pleasant by choice? ... Forgo.

gre.s: Determined to finish her dissertation by spring, the doctoral student chose to ____ the holiday trip her friends had planned, staying behind in the library instead.
gre.clue: staying behind in the library instead

example: To pay her younger brother's school fees, Shirin decided to forgo new clothes for Eid two years in a row.

en: To make or do something on the spot without planning ahead
hook: IMPROVISE: IM-PRO-VISE, not foreseen (pro-vise), done on the spot.
story: Improvise. To make or do something on the spot without planning ahead. Halfway through Isaac's sister's wedding party, the power went out and the music died. Then Isaac grabbed a steel pot and a spoon, his cousins started clapping, and the aunties began singing old wedding songs. Everyone [laugh] danced harder than before. They had improvised a whole band in two minutes. Im means not, and provise is from the Latin for foreseen, as in provide, so to improvise is to act without foreseeing. So, what verb means to make something up on the spot? ... Improvise.

gre.s: When the main speaker failed to arrive, the host was forced to ____, delivering a twenty-minute talk with no notes at all.
gre.clue: with no notes at all

example: When the tent pole snapped during the camping trip, Farhan improvised a replacement from a bamboo stick and some rope.

en: Done carelessly, without choosing or judging with care
hook: IN-DISCRIMINATE: doesn't DISCRIMINATE, doesn't choose carefully.
story: Indiscriminate. Done carelessly, without choosing or judging with care. Every evening, Anna watched her uncle forward dozens of messages to the family group: health tips, fake news, old jokes and photos of flowers, all without reading them first. One day he forwarded a scam, and two cousins nearly lost money. Anna gently asked him to be less indiscriminate. To discriminate is to choose carefully between things, so indiscriminate means not choosing at all, just grabbing everything. So, what word describes careless action done without judgment? ... Indiscriminate.

gre.s: Critics condemned the ____ bombing campaign, which struck hospitals and markets as readily as military targets.
gre.clue: struck hospitals and markets as readily as military targets

example: Doctors warn that the indiscriminate use of antibiotics, often bought without a prescription, is breeding bacteria that no drug can kill.

en: Curious; eager for knowledge
hook: INQUISITIVE: always INQUIRING.
story: Inquisitive. Curious; eager for knowledge. Four-year-old Archie never stops asking questions. Why is the sky blue? Why do ducks not get wet? Where does the rain go after it falls? His grandmother answers every one patiently, and when she does not know, she says, "Let us find out together." An inquisitive child keeps the whole family thinking. Inquisitive comes from inquire, to ask, so an inquisitive person is always inquiring. So, what word describes a child who is curious about everything? ... Inquisitive.

gre.s: Endlessly ____, the young scientist pestered her mentors with questions and spent her weekends dismantling old instruments to learn how they worked.
gre.clue: pestered her mentors with questions

example: An inquisitive reader, my grandfather filled the margins of his books with questions he planned to look up later.

en: Deserving praise or reward
hook: MERITORIOUS: full of MERIT.
story: Meritorious. Deserving praise or reward. During the floods, a young boatman named Rudy made trip after trip through the rising water, carrying old people and children to the school shelter. He did not stop for two days, even when his hands blistered. Later, the district honoured him with an award for meritorious service. Rudy only said he had done what any neighbour would do. Meritorious means full of merit, deserving praise. So, what word describes an action that deserves honour and reward? ... Meritorious.

gre.s: The committee rejected his nomination, arguing that his work, while competent, was not especially ____ and did nothing to distinguish him from his peers.
gre.clue: did nothing to distinguish him from his peers

example: The fire officer received a medal for meritorious service after pulling six workers from the burning garment factory in Ashulia.

en: Someone overly absorbed in admiring themselves and their looks
hook: NARCISSUS: fell in love with his own reflection.
story: Narcissist. Someone overly absorbed in admiring themselves and their looks. At a cousin's wedding, Sienna noticed one guest who spent the whole evening taking selfies. He checked his hair in every mirror, posted forty photos of himself, and never once asked the bride how she was. Sienna [chuckle] whispered to her sister that he was a true narcissist. In the Greek myth, Narcissus fell in love with his own reflection in a pool, and a narcissist does much the same. So, what word names someone obsessed with admiring himself? ... Narcissist.

gre.s: A thoroughgoing ____, the actor treated every interview as an occasion for self-praise and could rarely sit through a conversation that was not about himself.
gre.clue: could rarely sit through a conversation that was not about himself

example: Only a narcissist would turn a friend's wedding toast into ten minutes about his own career, the guests muttered afterward.

en: Calm and peaceful; not easily upset
hook: PLACID: a PLACE that's calm, like a still lake.
story: Placid. Calm and peaceful; not easily upset. On a still winter morning, the mountain lake lies so placid that the green hills appear twice, once against the sky and once upside down in the water. Ralph's grandmother is like that lake. Even when the rice burns or the grandchildren shout, she smiles and fixes things. Her placid nature calms everyone around her. Placid is a cousin of placate, which means to calm someone down. So, what word describes a calm lake, or a calm person who is not easily upset? ... Placid.

gre.s: Despite the chaos surrounding him, the pilot remained ____, calmly guiding the damaged plane to a safe landing.
gre.clue: calmly guiding the damaged plane

example: Even when the toddlers screamed and threw rice across the table, their placid grandmother simply carried on with her story.

en: An expression of extreme enthusiasm; a free-form piece of music
hook: RHAPSODY: Bohemian RHAPSODY — wild, joyful music.
story: Rhapsody. An expression of extreme enthusiasm; also, a free-form piece of music. After her first trip to the mangrove forest, Talia could not stop talking. At dinner she went into a rhapsody about the spotted deer, the silent mangroves at dawn, and a tiger's pawprint she saw in the mud. Her father [laugh] put down his fork and said he would book the next trip himself. To rhapsodize is to speak with wild delight, like music flowing freely, as in the famous song Bohemian Rhapsody. So, what word names a burst of joyful, enthusiastic praise? ... Rhapsody.

gre.s: The critic, usually so restrained, launched into a ____ about the young violinist, praising her tone and phrasing in such ecstatic terms that readers were astonished.
gre.clue: in such ecstatic terms

example: Her travel blog dissolved into a rhapsody about the tea gardens of Srimangal, with three paragraphs devoted to the morning mist alone.

en: A split or division between groups, often over beliefs
hook: SCHISM (pronounced SIZ-um): a SCISSOR-cut through a group.
story: Schism. A split or division between groups, often over beliefs. Craig's university drama club had been close for years. Then a fierce argument broke out over whether to perform only local plays or translations of Shakespeare too. Friends stopped speaking, and by the end of the year there were two separate clubs rehearsing in different halls. The schism lasted three years, until a new president brought them back together. Schism comes from the Greek for split, and a schism splits a group in two. So, what word names a split within a group over beliefs? ... Schism.

gre.s: What began as a minor disagreement over doctrine eventually produced a lasting ____ within the movement, as its followers divided into two hostile camps.
gre.clue: as its followers divided into two hostile camps

example: A schism in the chess club over whether to allow speed games led half its members to start a rival group across town.

en: Morally ignoble or dishonorable; dirty and squalid
hook: SORDID: SORE and DIRTY.
story: Sordid. Morally ignoble or dishonourable; also, dirty and squalid. When a newspaper investigated a factory owner, the details were sordid: unpaid wages, fake safety certificates, and bribes to inspectors so the cracked walls would be ignored. Workers who complained were quietly fired. Meg, a young reporter, felt sick as she typed the story late at night. Sordid comes from the Latin for dirt, and a sordid affair is morally filthy. So, what word describes a scandal that is shameful, dirty and dishonourable? ... Sordid.

gre.s: The memoir, which promised an inspiring tale of artistic triumph, instead revealed a ____ history of bribery, betrayal, and blackmail.
gre.clue: bribery, betrayal, and blackmail

example: Journalists spent months tracing the sordid deals through which public land in Dhaka was quietly sold to friends of officials.

en: More than needed; unnecessary
hook: SUPER-FLUOUS: flows (flu) OVER (super) the top.
story: Superfluous. More than needed; unnecessary. Before his trip to the beach, Zach packed six shirts, three pairs of shoes, a heavy jacket and an umbrella. His sister [chuckle] unpacked half of it. "It is the beach in April," she said, "and the jacket is superfluous." He went with one small bag and never missed a thing. Super means over and fluous means flowing, so superfluous things overflow beyond what you need. So, what word describes something extra and unnecessary? ... Superfluous.

gre.s: The editor cut several paragraphs that she considered ____, since they merely repeated points made earlier in the chapter.
gre.clue: merely repeated points made earlier

example: Apologizing again would be superfluous, Mitu decided, since her sister had already forgiven her the night before.

en: Very weak or slight
hook: TENUOUS: as THIN as a thread.
story: Tenuous. Very weak or slight. In a storm on the coast, Roger's fishing boat broke loose from the jetty, held only by a thin, fraying rope. He grabbed it just as the last strands began to split. The link was so tenuous that one more wave would have taken the boat. Years later, his son met the word in a GRE passage about a tenuous argument, and he smiled: an argument, like a rope, can hang by a thread. Tenuous comes from the Latin for thin. So, what word describes a link or argument that is very weak? ... Tenuous.

gre.s: The prosecutor's case rested on a ____ chain of circumstantial evidence, and the defense easily broke it by showing that the key witness had been miles away.
gre.clue: the defense easily broke it

example: The village's tenuous internet connection dropped every few minutes, making Rakib's online exam a test of patience as much as knowledge.

en: Real; used to emphasize that a description is accurate
hook: VERITABLE: VERY TRUE (veritas = truth).
story: Veritable. Real; used to emphasize that a description is accurate. When Ingrid's grandmother cooked for the holiday, the kitchen became a veritable factory. Three stoves burned at once, pots of biryani and korma bubbled side by side, and four aunts chopped onions in a row. By noon there was food for two hundred guests. Calling it a factory was no exaggeration; it was a veritable one. Veritable comes from veritas, the Latin for truth, as in verify. So, what word means truly deserving a description, real in every sense? ... Veritable.

gre.s: The once-neglected archive has become a ____ goldmine for historians: scholars have already uncovered hundreds of documents previously thought lost.
gre.clue: scholars have already uncovered hundreds of documents previously thought lost

example: Grandma's kitchen became a veritable factory before Eid, turning out hundreds of pitha for relatives, neighbors, and the night guards.

en: Showing great energy and enthusiasm for a cause or goal
hook: ZEALOUS: full of ZEAL (passion).
story: Zealous. Showing great energy and enthusiasm for a cause or goal. Every Saturday, a group of students gathers at the city beach with gloves and sacks to pick up plastic. Their leader, Nadia, arrives first and leaves last, and she has convinced half her university to join. Even in the rain, she sings as she works. Nobody is more zealous about clean beaches. Zealous means full of zeal, which is burning enthusiasm. So, what word describes someone full of eager energy for a cause? ... Zealous.

gre.s: The new inspector was so ____ in enforcing the regulations that he fined shops for violations his predecessors had ignored for years.
gre.clue: fined shops for violations his predecessors had ignored for years

example: A zealous volunteer, Imran spent every weekend of the dengue season knocking on doors to warn families about standing water.
